steps.title: Growth on growth
steps.body: €10,000 grows by 5% every year. Each year, last year's growth grows too. This is called [[compound-interest]]. After 30 years, there is about €43,000. In the first years, the effect is small. After many years, it becomes large.

steps.prompt: €10,000 must wait 18 years, for example for a child's studies. Choose where it waits, and see what happens.

choices.label: All in a savings account at 1.5%
choices.ending: After 18 years, you have €13,100. The value never fell. But prices rose too. With prices rising 2% a year, the money buys what about €9,100 buys today.

choices.label: Half in a savings account, half in a fund that invests all over the world
choices.ending: After 18 years, you have €18,600. In year six, the value fell to €10,900. That fall was half as deep as with all of the money in the fund.

choices.label: All in a fund that invests all over the world
choices.ending: After 18 years, you have €24,100. But in year six, the value fell to €10,800. This only works for money that can wait. The next 18 years may look very different.

steps.prompt: €10,000 grows by 5% a year. Each year's growth also grows. How much is there after 18 years?
steps.reveal: About €24,000. It is not €10,000 + 18 × €500 = €19,000. From the second year on, the earlier growth also grows. This is [[compound-interest]].

steps.prompt: True or false: with compound interest, money grows by the same amount every year.
steps.explanation: False. Each year, the earnings from earlier years earn too. So the amount added each year gets bigger.

steps.prompt: Why does time matter so much for compound interest?
options: Earnings on earlier earnings get bigger every year
The bank pays a bonus after 10 years
Prices stop rising after many years
steps.explanation: Compound interest is slow at first and fast later. The longer money can wait, the bigger the difference between the paths.

steps.title: Your interest grows too
steps.body: Your savings account holds **{savingsBalance}** and pays **{savingsRate}** a year. The bank adds the interest to your balance. The next year, that interest earns interest too. What your money gains after rising prices is called your [[real-return]].

steps.prompt: Your savings account holds {savingsBalance} at {savingsRate} a year. Move the sliders to see what it could grow to after some years.

goal.hint: Move a slider to see the result change.

steps.note: The amount and the rate start at your real numbers. This is an example, not a forecast. It does not count rising prices.

scenes.title: Growth on growth
scenes.desc: Each year, the earlier growth grows too. After many years, the effect is large.

captions.text: Each year, last year's growth grows too.
